title: Permissions in a client portal
metaTitle: Show a client what they can open
excerpt: Show a client which files they can open, and why one is unavailable. A missing download with no reason feels like a bug. A sentence that names the reason feels like care.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, a route where the closed lane should be marked.
caption: If the way is closed, the sign should say so before the turn. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a portal hide files a client cannot download?
faqs.answer: Hide files from other clients, and for a file this client expects, show it and say why the download is unavailable, such as not shared yet, view only, or replaced. A missing file looks like you forgot. A labeled file looks like a decision.

faqs.question: What should a guest on the client's team see?
faqs.answer: Only the projects and files the client explicitly shared with them. The screen should say whose access they have, in plain language. If they can comment and not delete, show comment and say delete is not theirs. A hidden download they were promised in a forwarded email will be reported as a broken portal.

faqs.question: When should the reason appear?
faqs.answer: Before they tap, on the file row. Waiting until after a failed download wastes their time and reads as a glitch. View only, with the reason, belongs where the download button would have been. The same sentence should appear if they try anyway.

markdown:
Client portal permissions UX is how a client, looking for the file they were promised, learns what they can do with it and why something is unavailable. Show the file. Say the limit. A hidden download feels like a bug. They will refresh, try another browser, and then write to you convinced the portal lost the work.

Other clients' files are the exception. Those stay hidden. This article is about the files this person reasonably expects, because you named them, and about the actions on those files: open, download, comment, replace.

## What they can do with the promised file

They should see three answers on the row. Can I open it? Can I download it? If one of those is no, why?

Open and download are different permissions, and clients feel the difference. View only can be legitimate while you are still replacing a file, or while a mark is not cleared to travel. If that is the rule, the row says View only, and the download control is visible and unavailable, with the reason. Removing the download with no sentence looks like the button failed to render.

Comment, approve, and upload are separate verbs. If they can comment and not delete the studio's file, show comment and do not show a delete that 404s. If they can upload a reference and not overwrite the delivered file, say where the upload will go. "This will be added as a reference. It will not replace the logo pack." That sentence prevents a nasty surprise on both sides.

The W3C describes the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a shared bar for perceivable, operable, understandable interfaces. A missing control is not understandable. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is a useful check before you ship a file row that only reveals actions on hover. Hover does not exist on the phone they will use in the taxi. The reason has to be text on the row.

## Hide, disable, or explain

Hide other clients, other projects they were not invited to, and the studio's internal notes. A disabled button labeled "Acme's brand files" on Beta's portal is a leak with a lock icon. Absence is the correct design across clients. Test it with two real accounts. Do not trust a filter you have not tried to break.

Disable and explain actions on files they can see and cannot complete. Download while view only. Approve while you asked them only to read. Invite a teammate if only one admin on their side can invite. The control stays where they look, it does not fire, and one sentence names the condition.

Explain with no button when there is nothing to press yet. "The logo pack is not shared yet. It will show up here when it is." The row can exist because you mentioned it, or the empty project can say it. What you must not do is mention the file in email and then present a portal with no trace of it. They will not interpret that as process. They will interpret it as a mistake.

The accidental state is a file that loads for the studio and vanishes for the client because a share flag was off. From the client side that is a hidden file. From the studio side everything looks fine. The permission UI has to show the studio, on the file, that the client cannot see it. A badge, "Not visible to the client," in the studio view, prevents the email that says it is ready when it is not.

## Rules a client will actually hit

Not shared yet. The studio is still working. The client was told "it's in the portal" a little early. The portal should be able to show a placeholder with the name and "Not shared yet," or the studio should not send the email. Pick one workflow and write the sentence. Hope is not a workflow.

View only. They can read on screen and cannot take the file away. Say whether that is temporary. "View only until we replace the type" is a reason. "View only" alone is a puzzle they will try to route around with screenshots. If screenshots are fine, you may not need the restriction. If they are not, the reason should say what you need them to wait for.

Replaced. The old file remains for the record, and the current file is the one they can treat as final. Mark current clearly. If they cannot download the retired file, say it is kept for reference on screen. Do not leave two downloads with the same weight.

Teammates. A client admin can invite a colleague. The colleague sees this project only. Say that at the invite and again when the colleague lands. "You can view the Hanabi project for Northwind. You cannot see other projects." Use the real project name. A generic "limited access" teaches them nothing, and they will click around looking for the rest.

Studio versus client actions. Clients should not see "publish to portal," billing tools for the studio, or internal assignees. Those belong in the studio session. If you use one component library for both, hide the studio actions by session, not by a CSS class someone will forget. A client who can open your publish dialog will publish something you did not review.

## Say it before they need the file in the room

The worst time to reveal a permission is when they are already presenting. The row had a download icon. The tap failed. The room is waiting. Put view only on the row in the morning, when they first open the portal, so they can ask you before the meeting.

Use the same sentence in the email if you know the limit. "In the portal, the pack is view only until Friday." Then the portal repeats it. Two channels, one policy. If the email says download and the portal refuses, the portal looks broken even though the rule is real. Change the email or change the rule.

Do not lecture. One line on the row, and a longer note only if they tap for it. "View only while we correct the mark" is enough. A paragraph about intellectual property on every file will not be read, and it will push the filename down. The filename is the promise. Keep it high.

If a file is hidden from some teammates and not others, the person who cannot see it should not get a tease that names a secret document. "You do not have any files in this folder" is safer than "You cannot see the acquisition memo." Sensitivity applies to the denial too.

## The studio view is part of the permission

Whoever shares the file needs to see the client's view before they send the link. A preview as the client, using the client's actual rights, should be one action on the file. If the preview still shows studio controls, it is not a preview.

Show a short access line in the studio UI. Visible to Ada and Sam. View only. Not visible to the client yet. Those states should be dull and readable, not a permission matrix of checkboxes with no preview. The matrix will be set wrong. The preview is harder to set wrong.

When you remove access, the file should disappear for them on refresh, and their next visit should not be a raw error. "This file is no longer shared" is a permission message. A 403 page with no project name is an error pretending to be a policy. You already have an error article. Use the policy sentence here so the error template stays for real failures.

Search has to obey the same visibility. A file they cannot see should not appear in their search. A file they can see but not download should appear with the same view-only sentence. That is the next piece, and it is where leaks like to hide, because search is a second door.


Invite links are permissions with a clock on them. If a teammate invite expires, the page should say which project it was for, in the name they were told, and how to ask for a fresh invite. A raw token failure looks like the portal is down. The person who invited them should see pending invites beside People, and should be able to revoke one without calling the studio. If only the studio can invite, say that on the client's people list so they do not hunt for a button you removed.
## Review with two clients and one guest

Create two clients. Share a file with one. Confirm the other cannot search it, open it by URL, or see its name in a notification. Create a guest with view-only access. Confirm the download is explained, not missing. Confirm the guest cannot open the second project by editing the link.

Read the row on a phone. The reason should be visible without a hover and without a tap. If it is only in a tooltip, it is not shipped.

Then try search, because they will. The next piece is [search inside a client portal](/blog/search-inside-a-client-portal). Results are part of the permission, not a loophole beside it.

If the portal should make access obvious to the client and to the studio, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). A file that is "in the portal" only for the person who uploaded it is not in the portal yet.
